question: Can I make du'a in sujud during an obligatory prayer, and can that du'a be in any language?
asked: Can she make du'a in the sajdah of the fard salah, or is it only allowed in the nafl salah? And if so, can the du'a be done in any language?
answer:
So as with almost every question on this paper, and every question that's ever asked of a scholar: nobody asks how many times a Muslim prays, because I'll say five and there's no difference. Nobody asks what direction we face; I'll say the qiblah, and there's no difference of opinion. Generally speaking, when people ask questions, they're asking about the gray areas. When there are gray areas, you're going to find interpretations, and so this is one of those gray areas. In today's Q&A, I'm just giving you what I think is the strongest opinion, without going into the counter-opinions and counter-evidences.

The sister says, can she make du'a in the sajdah of the fard, and can she make that du'a in any language? The response: yes, yes, yes, yes. **She may make du'a in any sajdah and in any language.** There is no restriction from the hadith about making du'a, and there is no restriction from the Qur'an and Sunnah about the language of du'a. And the second point is that, by unanimous consensus, you may make du'a in any language. But the problem would come within salah. Some of our scholars are very restrictive, and they say the salah, from the iftitah, from Allahu Akbar to the taslim, should be all in Arabic. And I understand that sentiment, but there is no evidence for this.

And our Prophet ﷺ, when he encouraged people to make du'a, obviously he's speaking to a group of Arabs, but he knows that his message is going to be given to the non-Arabs as well, and he knows that the Ummah is going to increase manifold. And he didn't say, "Oh, but by the way, this is only for Arabic." Nor did he say, "Restrict yourselves to the du'a that you are taught in the Qur'an and Sunnah." He left it open. And he said that when you are in the state of sajdah, then increase your du'a, because the chances of your du'a being answered are very high. And he left it open.

This means... there are many different dialects of Arabic. And to this day, when a person makes du'a, the one who makes du'a in Moroccan Arabic is very different than the one who makes du'a in Iraqi Arabic, versus the one who makes du'a in Saudi Arabic, versus one who makes du'a in Egyptian Arabic. And if you know these different dialects, you will know that the differences are almost as much as between some of the languages even, because they're so radically different. Those who don't understand are very simplistic. They say du'a can only be made in Arabic. And I respond to them: which Arabic do you mean? Egyptian Arabic, Syrian Arabic, Kuwaiti Arabic, Yemeni Arabic, Moroccan Arabic? They are so different.

In fact, the Arabic that the Prophet ﷺ used to speak, the classical Arabic, is no longer spoken anywhere as a living language. And everybody who studies Arabic knows this, right? It's nothing new that I'm teaching; it's just a fact. No group of Arabs speak classical Arabic amongst themselves, as a family, as a society. Only in bubbles of Islamic seminaries. When I went to the University of Medina, some of our teachers would speak in classical Arabic, but even then, usually they would just revert to the Saudi dialect when they were teaching. Only when we were quoting Qur'an and Sunnah would they actually be forced to, because that is in classical Arabic. Imagine Shakespeare versus modern English. Shakespeare is only 500 years old; the Arabic of the Sahabah is 1400 years old. Can you imagine the difference?

My point being, why is all of this here? When some scholar, a non-Arab usually, when a non-Arab says you must make du'a in Arabic, you respond to him: the Arabic of today is almost incomprehensible compared to the Arabic of the classical times. Most modern Arabs, when they open up the Qur'an, understand maybe 40 to 50%, 60% at max. They don't understand the whole Qur'an. And the hadith even more so.

The point being, this notion of our du'as and our prayers being restricted only to Arabic: no. What is in Arabic? The Qur'an, yes. When we recite al-Fatihah, it should be in Arabic. What is in Arabic? The adhkar of salah: "Subhana Rabbiyal A'la," "Rabbana wa lakal hamd," "Allahu Akbar." You say that in Arabic. Other than this, when it comes time for du'a, you may make du'a in any language, and you may make du'a in any salah: fard salah, Sunnah salah, nafl salah, tahajjud salah, witr salah. No problem. When you go into sajdah, after you say "Subhana Rabbiyal A'la, Subhana Rabbiyal A'la, Subhana Rabbiyal A'la," you make du'a, and you make du'a from the heart, and you make du'a in any language. No problem whatsoever. And may I encourage all of you to make du'a, especially in the tahajjud salah or the taraweeh salah in the nights of Ramadan.
